claim: Human vision has striking radial asymmetries, with performance on many tasks varying sharply with stimulus polar angle.
source: Human vision has striking radial asymmetries, with performance on many tasks varying sharply with stimulus polar angle.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by multiple citations throughout the manuscript and behavioral data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Performance is generally better on the horizontal than vertical meridian.
source: Performance is generally better on the horizontal than vertical meridian
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1 and cited literature.

claim: Performance is better on the lower than upper vertical meridian.
source: and on the lower than upper vertical meridian
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1 and cited literature.

claim: Radial asymmetries decrease gradually with deviation from the vertical meridian.
source: and these asymmetries decrease gradually with deviation from the vertical meridian.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 1C-F showing gradual changes with angular distance.

claim: Cortical magnification in human primary visual cortex varies substantially around the visual field.
source: We show that cortical magnification in the human primary visual cortex, measured in 163 subjects, varies substantially around the visual field, with a pattern similar to behavior.
evidence: Supported by measurements from 163 subjects shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cortical magnification was measured in 163 subjects.
source: measured in 163 subjects
evidence: Direct statement about sample size.

claim: Cortical magnification varies with a pattern similar to behavior.
source: with a pattern similar to behavior.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Radial asymmetries in the cortex are larger than those found in the retina.
source: These radial asymmetries in the cortex are larger than those found in the retina
evidence: Supported by comparative data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Radial asymmetries are correlated between monozygotic twin pairs.
source: and they are correlated between monozygotic twin pairs.
evidence: Supported by twin correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is a tight link between cortical topography and behavior.
source: These findings indicate a tight link between cortical topography and behavior
evidence: Inference drawn from the correlation between cortical measurements and behavioral performance.

claim: Visual field asymmetries are partly heritable.
source: and suggest that visual field asymmetries are partly heritable.
evidence: Inferred from twin correlation data showing higher correlations in monozygotic twins.

claim: At the center of gaze, we see fine details whereas in the periphery acuity is about 50 times lower.
source: At the center of gaze, we see fine details whereas in the periphery acuity is about 50 times lower (Frisén and Glansholm, 1975).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frisén and Glansholm, 1975.

claim: The eccentricity effect is mediated by a far greater density of cone photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cells for the fovea than periphery.
source: This eccentricity effect is mediated by a far greater density of cone photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) for the fovea than periphery, as well as by a correspondingly greater amount of cortical surface area per degree of the visual field (Rodieck, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodieck, 1998.

claim: Visual performance varies as a function of polar angle at matched eccentricity.
source: Importantly, visual performance varies not only across eccentricity, but also as a function of polar angle (Figure 1); at matched eccentricity, performance is better along the horizontal than the vertical meridian (horizontal-vertical asymmetry, or 'anisotropy'; HVA) and better along the lower than the upper vertical meridian (vertical meridian asymmetry; VMA) (Carrasco et al., 2001; Cameron et al., 2002; Montaser-Kouhsari and Carrasco, 2009; Corbett and Carrasco, 2011; Abrams et al., 2012; Baldwin et al., 2012; Greenwood et al., 2017; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Barbot et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and Figure 1 showing behavioral data.

claim: Radial asymmetries are present in contrast sensitivity.
source: These asymmetries are present in several basic perceptual dimensions, including contrast sensitivity (Rovamo and Virsu, 1979; Kroon and van der Wildt, 1980; Robson and Graham, 1981; Regan and Beverley, 1983; Pointer and Hess, 1989; Carrasco et al., 2001; Cameron et al., 2002; Fuller et al., 2008; Corbett and Carrasco, 2011; Abrams et al., 2012; Baldwin et al., 2012; Rosén et al., 2014; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Purokayastha et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Radial asymmetries are present in spatial resolution.
source: and spatial resolution (Anderson et al., 1992; Mackeben, 1999; Altpeter et al., 2000; Carrasco et al., 2002; Talgar and Carrasco, 2002; Montaser-Kouhsari and Carrasco, 2009; Wilkinson et al., 2016; Greenwood et al., 2017; Barbot et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Variations in performance around the visual field can be as pronounced as that of doubling the stimulus eccentricity.
source: Variations in performance around the visual field are substantial: they can be as pronounced as that of doubling the stimulus eccentricity (Carrasco et al., 2001; Barbot et al., 2019; Himmelberg et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies quantifying the magnitude of asymmetries.

claim: Radial asymmetries are in retinal coordinates.
source: Moreover, these asymmetries are in retinal coordinates: the shape of the performance fields are constant in head-centered (but not screen-centered) coordinates whether subjects are tested with their heads tilted or straight (Corbett and Carrasco, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Corbett and Carrasco, 2011.

claim: The radial asymmetries likely arise relatively early in the visual processing stream.
source: This result suggests that the effects likely arise relatively early in the visual processing stream.
evidence: Inference based on the finding that asymmetries are in retinal coordinates.

claim: Both the HVA and the VMA become more pronounced as target eccentricity increases.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, radial asymmetries vary with several low-level stimulus properties: in general, both the HVA and the VMA become more pronounced as target eccentricity, target spatial frequency, or number of distractors increase (Carrasco et al., 2001; Cameron et al., 2002; Baldwin et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies examining stimulus properties.

claim: Both the HVA and the VMA become more pronounced as target spatial frequency increases.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, radial asymmetries vary with several low-level stimulus properties: in general, both the HVA and the VMA become more pronounced as target eccentricity, target spatial frequency, or number of distractors increase (Carrasco et al., 2001; Cameron et al., 2002; Baldwin et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies examining stimulus properties.

claim: Both the HVA and the VMA become more pronounced as number of distractors increase.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, radial asymmetries vary with several low-level stimulus properties: in general, both the HVA and the VMA become more pronounced as target eccentricity, target spatial frequency, or number of distractors increase (Carrasco et al., 2001; Cameron et al., 2002; Baldwin et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies examining stimulus properties.

claim: Radial asymmetries are largest at the cardinal meridians.
source: These radial asymmetries are not general hemifield or quarterfield effects; they are largest at the cardinal meridians and decrease gradually as the angular distance from the vertical meridian increases (Abrams et al., 2012; Baldwin et al., 2012; Barbot et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies examining angular specificity.

claim: Performance in many tasks is similar across all visual quadrants at 45° intercardinal locations.
source: Indeed, performance in many tasks is similar across all visual quadrants at 45° intercardinal locations (Carrasco et al., 2001; Cameron et al., 2002; Corbett and Carrasco, 2011; Abrams et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Variation in the accuracy of a computational observer classifier in terms of retinal cell density was small compared to measured performance differences with polar angle in human observers.
source: Variation in the accuracy of the classifier in terms of cell density was small compared to the measured performance differences with polar angle in human observers.
evidence: Based on computational modeling results from Kupers et al., 2019; Kupers et al., 2020.

claim: Substantial additional radial asymmetries must arise in visual processing efferent from the retina—i.e., the LGN or cortex.
source: Substantial additional radial asymmetries must therefore arise in visual processing efferent from the retina—i.e., the LGN or cortex.
evidence: Inference based on computational modeling showing retinal factors are insufficient.

claim: Within ±10° of the meridians, the surface area is ~80% greater for the horizontal than the vertical representation.
source: For example, within ±10° of the meridians, the surface area is ~80% greater for the horizontal than the vertical representation (Figure 2B and D)
evidence: Directly measured from the HCP dataset and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Within ±10° of the meridians, the surface area is ~80% greater for the lower than the upper meridian.
source: and for the lower than the upper meridian (Figure 2C and E).
evidence: Directly measured from the HCP dataset and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Within ±10° ROIs, 94% of the 163 subjects have positive HVAs.
source: Within these ±10° ROIs, 94% of the 163 subjects have positive HVAs
evidence: Statistical summary of individual subject data.

claim: Within ±10° ROIs, 93% of the 163 subjects have positive VMAs.
source: and 93% have positive VMAs.
evidence: Statistical summary of individual subject data.

claim: The asymmetries are largest for narrow wedge ROIs.
source: The asymmetries are largest for narrow wedge ROIs.
evidence: Observed pattern in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The VMA decreases more sharply with distance than the HVA.
source: They decrease gradually with angular distance from the vertical meridian, with the VMA decreasing more sharply with distance than the HVA.
evidence: Observed pattern in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Previous estimates of V1 cortical magnification by Horton and Hoyt, 1991 fall about halfway between measures for the vertical and horizontal meridians.
source: Previous estimates of V1 cortical magnification by Horton and Hoyt, 1991 fall about halfway between our measures for the vertical and horizontal meridians as they did not account for angular variation (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Comparison with published model shown in Figure 2B.

claim: V1 mid-gray surface area measured from the HCP dataset is highly correlated with spatial frequency thresholds measured by Barbot et al., 2021 in matched ROIs.
source: V1 mid-gray surface area measured from the HCP dataset (Benson et al., 2018) is highly correlated with the spatial frequency thresholds measured by Barbot et al., 2021 in matched ROIs.
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Pearson correlation between V1 surface area and spatial frequency thresholds is 0.99.
source: The Pearson correlation is 0.99.
evidence: Statistical result from correlation analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: V1 surface area and acuity threshold covary with polar angle.
source: Our finding that V1 surface area and acuity threshold covary with polar angle (Figure 3) parallels findings that they covary with eccentricity (Duncan and Boynton, 2003).
evidence: Comparison with previous findings and data shown in Figure 3.

claim: For monozygotic twin pairs, the intraclass correlation of ROI asymmetry is ≥0.5 for most ROIs.
source: Indeed, for monozygotic twin pairs, the intraclass correlation (ICC) of ROI asymmetry in terms of the ROI's angular width is ≥0.5 for most ROIs (Figure 4).
evidence: Statistical analysis of twin data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Dizygotic twin pairs have correlations close to 0 for HVA.
source: Interestingly, dizygotic twin pairs have correlations close to 0 for HVA but positive correlations similar to those of the monozygotic twins for the VMA.
evidence: Statistical analysis of twin data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Dizygotic twin pairs have positive correlations similar to monozygotic twins for the VMA.
source: Interestingly, dizygotic twin pairs have correlations close to 0 for HVA but positive correlations similar to those of the monozygotic twins for the VMA.
evidence: Statistical analysis of twin data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Age- and gender-matched unrelated pairs have correlations for both HVA and VMA that are not statistically distinct from 0 for all ROIs.
source: Age- and gender-matched unrelated pairs have correlations for both HVA and VMA that are not statistically distinct from 0 for all ROIs.
evidence: Statistical analysis of unrelated pairs shown in Figure 4.

claim: The correlation of mean V1 thickness for monozygotic twins is 0.76.
source: In comparison, the correlation of mean V1 thickness for the same monozygotic and dizygotic twins is 0.76 and 0.11, respectively, with 68% CIs across 10,000 bootstraps of 0.67–0.82 and −0.07 to 0.29.
evidence: Statistical analysis of V1 thickness in twins.

claim: The correlation of mean V1 thickness for dizygotic twins is 0.11.
source: In comparison, the correlation of mean V1 thickness for the same monozygotic and dizygotic twins is 0.76 and 0.11, respectively, with 68% CIs across 10,000 bootstraps of 0.67–0.82 and −0.07 to 0.29.
evidence: Statistical analysis of V1 thickness in twins.

claim: For V1 mid-gray surface area, the correlation for monozygotic twins is 0.90.
source: For the V1 mid-gray surface area these correlations are 0.90 (68% CI: 0.88–0.93) and 0.71 (68% CI: 0.57–0.81), respectively.
evidence: Statistical analysis of V1 surface area in twins.

claim: For V1 mid-gray surface area, the correlation for dizygotic twins is 0.71.
source: For the V1 mid-gray surface area these correlations are 0.90 (68% CI: 0.88–0.93) and 0.71 (68% CI: 0.57–0.81), respectively.
evidence: Statistical analysis of V1 surface area in twins.

claim: The HVA and VMA may be controlled by different mechanisms.
source: The general pattern, however, whereby there is a large difference in correlation between monozygotic and dizygotic twins for the HVA, but not for the VMA, suggests a larger heritable component for the HVA, and that the HVA and VMA may be controlled by different mechanisms.
evidence: Inference based on differential twin correlations for HVA vs VMA.

claim: The cortical VMA and HVA do not differ substantially by sex.
source: We find that the cortical VMA and HVA do not differ substantially by sex or across age-groups (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: The cortical VMA and HVA do not differ substantially across age-groups.
source: We find that the cortical VMA and HVA do not differ substantially by sex or across age-groups (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: The HVA and VMA are similar in males and females in psychophysical findings.
source: This is consistent with psychophysical findings that the HVA and VMA are similar in males and females (Barbot et al., 2021; Purokayastha et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: The average size of V1 is about 10% larger in males.
source: Whereas the average size of V1 is about 10% larger in males, V1 size normalized to the entire cortical surface area is similar for males and females (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: Analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: V1 size normalized to the entire cortical surface area is similar for males and females.
source: Whereas the average size of V1 is about 10% larger in males, V1 size normalized to the entire cortical surface area is similar for males and females (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: Analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: Below 8° of eccentricity, cone density is greater on the horizontal than vertical meridian, with an HVA of ~20%.
source: Below 8° of eccentricity, cone density is greater on the horizontal than vertical meridian, with an HVA of ~20% (Figure 5A; Curcio et al., 1990).
evidence: Data from Curcio et al., 1990 shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Over the 0-8° eccentricity range, the HVA measures up to 40% in midget RGC density.
source: Over the same eccentricity range, the HVA measures up to 40% in midget RGC density and 60–80% in visual cortex.
evidence: Data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Over the 0-8° eccentricity range, the HVA measures 60–80% in visual cortex.
source: Over the same eccentricity range, the HVA measures up to 40% in midget RGC density and 60–80% in visual cortex.
evidence: Data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the 0-8° eccentricity range, the VMA of the cone density is 0 or slightly negative.
source: In this eccentricity range, the VMA of the cone density is 0 or slightly negative (Figure 5B): the upper visual field (inferior retina) has higher cone density than the lower visual field (superior retina), indicating that cone density cannot be the source of the behavioral VMA (Kupers et al., 2019).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 5B and citation to Kupers et al., 2019.

claim: Cone density cannot be the source of the behavioral VMA.
source: the upper visual field (inferior retina) has higher cone density than the lower visual field (superior retina), indicating that cone density cannot be the source of the behavioral VMA (Kupers et al., 2019).
evidence: Inference based on cone density data and citation to Kupers et al., 2019.

claim: The VMA becomes positive in midget RGC density (up to ~20%).
source: The VMA becomes positive in midget RGC density (up to ~20%) and still larger in the cortex (~40–100%).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The VMA is still larger in the cortex (~40–100%).
source: The VMA becomes positive in midget RGC density (up to ~20%) and still larger in the cortex (~40–100%).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The radial asymmetries are substantially larger in the cortex compared to both the cone photoreceptors and the mRGCs.
source: Hence, the radial asymmetries are substantially larger in the cortex compared to both the cone photoreceptors and the mRGCs.
evidence: Summary of comparative data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The differences in polar angle asymmetries across stages of processing vary with eccentricity in a manner that suggest new properties at each stage.
source: Note that neither the changes in polar angle asymmetries from cone density to mRGC density nor from mRGC density to cortex are simple scale factors; rather, the differences across stages of processing vary with eccentricity in a manner that suggest new properties at each stage.
evidence: Inference based on the pattern of data in Figure 5.

claim: Prior studies have shown radial asymmetries in visual cortex in fMRI BOLD amplitude.
source: Prior studies have also shown radial asymmetries in visual cortex, in fMRI BOLD amplitude (Liu et al., 2006; O'Connell et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Prior studies have shown radial asymmetries in visual cortex in cortical volume.
source: in cortical volume (O'Connell et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Prior studies have shown radial asymmetries in cortical magnification in human.
source: in cortical magnification in human (Silva et al., 2018) and Macaque monkey (Van Essen et al., 1984)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Prior studies have shown radial asymmetries in cortical magnification in Macaque monkey.
source: in cortical magnification in human (Silva et al., 2018) and Macaque monkey (Van Essen et al., 1984)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Prior studies have shown radial asymmetries in pRF size in human.
source: in pRF size in human (Silva et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Prior studies have shown radial asymmetries in spatial frequency preference in human.
source: in spatial frequency preference in human (Aghajari et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Prior studies have shown radial asymmetries in diffusion MRI in human.
source: and in diffusion MRI in human (O'Connell et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: O'Connell et al., 2016 found that a greater volume of visual cortex is activated by lower than upper hemifield stimuli.
source: For instance, O'Connell et al., 2016 found that a greater volume of visual cortex is activated by lower than upper hemifield stimuli.
evidence: Supported by citation to specific finding.

claim: Silva et al., 2018 quantified cortical magnification in visual field quadrants for V1–V3 and reported a greater magnification in the horizontal than the vertical quadrants and in the lower than the upper quadrant.
source: Silva et al., 2018 quantified cortical magnification in visual field quadrants (lower, upper, left, and right) for V1–V3 and reported a greater magnification in the horizontal than the vertical quadrants and in the lower than the upper quadrant.
evidence: Supported by citation to specific findings.

claim: Neither behavior nor cortical magnification is uniform within quadrants.
source: However, neither behavior (Carrasco et al., 2001; Cameron et al., 2002; Abrams et al., 2012; Baldwin et al., 2012; Barbot et al., 2021) nor cortical magnification is uniform within quadrants (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by citations and data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cortical surface area is the most direct measure of cortical asymmetry and most invariant to changes in experimental details.
source: In this study, we chose to emphasize cortical surface area as our measure of cortical asymmetry rather than pRF size or BOLD amplitude. Whereas all of these measures reflect important properties of visual system organization, we consider surface area, being closely tied to anatomy, to provide the most direct interpretation and to be most invariant to changes in experimental details.
evidence: Reasoning for methodological choice.

claim: BOLD amplitude is influenced by vascular density.
source: BOLD amplitude is influenced by a variety of non-neural factors, such as vascular density (Lee et al., 1995; Winawer et al., 2010; Kay et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on BOLD confounds.

claim: BOLD amplitude is influenced by cortical surface orientation relative to the MRI bore.
source: and cortical surface orientation relative to the MRI bore (Gagnon et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on BOLD confounds.

claim: pRF size is dependent on both neural receptive field size and the scatter of neural receptive field centers within a voxel.
source: PRF size is dependent on both neural receptive field size and the scatter of neural receptive field centers within a voxel (Amano et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on pRF properties.

claim: Regions with lower magnification would have a greater change in neural RF center across the voxel, and hence potentially larger pRFs even if neural RFs were matched.
source: The within-voxel scatter is influenced by cortical magnification, such that regions with lower magnification, like the vertical meridian, would have a greater change in neural RF center across the voxel, and hence potentially larger pRFs even if neural RFs were matched.
evidence: Inference about relationship between magnification and pRF size.

claim: pRF size is unlikely to influence surface area or magnification estimates, since these estimates are computed from pRF centers only.
source: In contrast, pRF size is unlikely to influence surface area or magnification estimates, since these estimates are computed from pRF centers only.
evidence: Reasoning about methodological independence.

claim: pRF size can be influenced by stimulus pattern.
source: Moreover, pRF size can be influenced by stimulus pattern (Le et al., 2017) and task (Kay et al., 2015; Klein et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on pRF properties.

claim: At 6° of eccentricity, the VMA and HVA in contrast sensitivity are >40%.
source: At 6° of eccentricity, the VMA and HVA in contrast sensitivity are >40% (Figure 1C, 0° vs. dotted-line; Figure 1E, upper vs. lower at 0°).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Both the HVA and VMA are present for stimuli of different orientation, size, luminance, eccentricity, and spatial frequency.
source: For example, both the HVA and VMA are present for stimuli of different orientation, size, luminance, eccentricity, and spatial frequency and under binocular and monocular viewing conditions (Carrasco et al., 2001; Cameron et al., 2002; Montaser-Kouhsari and Carrasco, 2009; Abrams et al., 2012; Baldwin et al., 2012; Corbett and Carrasco, 2011; Greenwood et al., 2017; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Barbot et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Both the HVA and VMA are present under binocular and monocular viewing conditions.
source: For example, both the HVA and VMA are present for stimuli of different orientation, size, luminance, eccentricity, and spatial frequency and under binocular and monocular viewing conditions (Carrasco et al., 2001; Cameron et al., 2002; Montaser-Kouhsari and Carrasco, 2009; Abrams et al., 2012; Baldwin et al., 2012; Corbett and Carrasco, 2011; Greenwood et al., 2017; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Barbot et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Radial asymmetries remain constant after both endogenous and exogenous covert attention have exerted their effects on perception.
source: They also remain constant after both endogenous (voluntary) (Purokayastha et al., 2021) and exogenous (involuntary) (Carrasco et al., 2001; Cameron et al., 2002) covert attention have exerted their effects on perception.
evidence: Supported by citations to attention studies.

claim: Attention improves performance in a variety of tasks at all polar angles to a similar degree but does not diminish the radial asymmetries.
source: That is, attention improves performance in a variety of tasks at all polar angles to a similar degree, for example, orientation discrimination and acuity, but does not diminish the radial asymmetries.
evidence: Supported by citations to attention studies.

claim: The shape of performance fields is maintained in visual short-term memory.
source: Furthermore, the shape of performance fields is maintained in visual short-term memory (VSTM), implying that the quality with which a visual stimulus is perceived and encoded at different locations affects the quality with which it is maintained in VSTM (Montaser-Kouhsari and Carrasco, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to VSTM study.

claim: Differential resources devoted to the different meridians in V1 may underlie both the perceptual and VSTM phenomena.
source: The results reported here—differential resources devoted to the different meridians in V1—may underlie both the perceptual and VSTM phenomena.
evidence: Inference connecting cortical findings to behavioral phenomena.

claim: The variance of resting-state fluctuations within the visual cortex has a strong genetic component.
source: The variance of resting-state fluctuations within the visual cortex has a strong genetic component (Yang et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: The surface areas of V1–V3 are more correlated for monozygotic than dizygotic twins.
source: and the surface areas of V1–V3 are more correlated for monozygotic than dizygotic twins (Alvarez et al., 2021; Benson et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Monozygotic twins had significantly higher correlations in HVA than dizygotic twins or unrelated pairs in all but the ±10° ROIs.
source: In all but the ±10° ROIs, monozygotic twins had significantly higher correlations in HVA than dizygotic twins or unrelated pairs (Figure 4).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is a strong genetic effect on HVA.
source: This finding is consistent with a strong genetic effect on HVA, a finding which might reflect a tendency for genetic factors to influence the topography of visual cortex more generally.
evidence: Inference based on twin correlation data.

claim: The VMA may be more influenced by environmental factors than the HVA.
source: This might be due to measurement limitations (the VMA is estimated from half as much data per subject as the HVA) or it might indicate a separate mechanism from HVA that is more influenced by environmental factors.
evidence: Speculation about the cause of differential twin correlations.

claim: Cortical magnification and visual task performance are greatest on the horizontal meridian, lesser on the lower vertical meridian, and the lowest on the upper vertical meridian.
source: To conclude, this study reveals a tight link between human perception around the visual field and the anatomical organization of V1: both cortical magnification and visual task performance are greatest on the horizontal meridian, lesser on the lower vertical meridian, and the lowest on the upper vertical meridian.
evidence: Summary of main findings from cortical and behavioral data.

claim: Both the behavioral and cortical HVA/VMA fall off gradually with angular distance from the cardinal meridians.
source: Both the behavioral and cortical HVA/VMA fall off gradually with angular distance from the cardinal meridians, with both performance and magnification reaching equality at the inter-cardinal angles.
evidence: Summary of main findings from cortical and behavioral data.

claim: Cortical asymmetries become more stark at multiple successive stages of the visual pathways.
source: Moreover, we show that these cortical asymmetries reflect the large-scale organization of the visual pathways, becoming more stark at multiple successive stages
evidence: Summary of findings comparing retina to cortex shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cortical asymmetries are highly correlated between monozygotic twin pairs.
source: and that they are highly correlated between monozygotic twin pairs.
evidence: Summary of twin correlation findings shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is a clear relation between biological structure and behavior.
source: These findings show a clear relation between biological structure and behavior
evidence: Inference based on correlation between cortical and behavioral measures.

claim: An increasingly large radial asymmetry across the visual system contributes to visual perception.
source: and reveal how an increasingly large radial asymmetry across the visual system contributes to visual perception.
evidence: Inference based on findings showing asymmetries increase from retina to cortex.

claim: Comprehensive models of vision must take into account performance and anatomical variations as a function of polar angle across iso-eccentric locations.
source: Comprehensive models of vision must take into account not only performance and anatomical variations across eccentricity, but also variations as a function of polar angle across iso-eccentric locations.
evidence: Recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: The HCP dataset includes 163 subjects with retinotopic maps and manually labeled iso-polar angle and iso-eccentricity contours.
source: To examine polar angle asymmetries in the cortical representation, we used a dataset of 163 subjects for whom retinotopic maps as well as manually labeled iso-polar angle and iso-eccentricity contours are publicly available.
evidence: Description of dataset used.

claim: The labeled data were produced by annotating the Human Connectome Project 7 Tesla Retinotopy Dataset.
source: These labeled data (Benson et al., 2021b) were produced by annotating the largest publicly available human retinotopy dataset: the Human Connectome Project (HCP) 7 Tesla Retinotopy Dataset (Benson et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of data source.

claim: All ROIs were restricted to 1–6° of eccentricity.
source: All ROIs were restricted to 1–6° of eccentricity.
evidence: Description of ROI definition.

claim: The VMA estimates measured surface area straddling the V1/V2 boundaries symmetrically to avoid potential artifacts from measuring receptive field centers near the vertical meridian.
source: For the VMA estimates, our measures of surface area straddled the V1/V2 boundaries symmetrically, as depicted in Figure 2A (right image, red and blue ROIs). We defined the ROIs this way to avoid potential artifacts that can arise from measuring receptive field centers near the vertical meridian, as discussed in prior reports (Larsson and Heeger, 2006; Winawer et al., 2010).
evidence: Methodological choice to avoid measurement artifacts.

claim: The correlation between V1 surface area and spatial frequency thresholds holds for surface areas calculated on the white-matter surface (r = 0.99).
source: This correlation holds for surface areas calculated on the white-matter surface (r = 0.99), the mid-gray surface (Figure 3; r = 0.99), and the pial surface (r = 0.98).
evidence: Statistical result from correlation analysis.

claim: The correlation between V1 surface area and spatial frequency thresholds holds for surface areas calculated on the mid-gray surface (r = 0.99).
source: This correlation holds for surface areas calculated on the white-matter surface (r = 0.99), the mid-gray surface (Figure 3; r = 0.99), and the pial surface (r = 0.98).
evidence: Statistical result from correlation analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The correlation between V1 surface area and spatial frequency thresholds holds for surface areas calculated on the pial surface (r = 0.98).
source: This correlation holds for surface areas calculated on the white-matter surface (r = 0.99), the mid-gray surface (Figure 3; r = 0.99), and the pial surface (r = 0.98).
evidence: Statistical result from correlation analysis.

claim: V1 surface area and acuity threshold covary with eccentricity.
source: Our finding that V1 surface area and acuity threshold covary with polar angle (Figure 3) parallels findings that they covary with eccentricity (Duncan and Boynton, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Motion sensitivity does not show the same systematic decline with eccentricity as acuity.
source: Other tasks such as motion sensitivity (McKee and Nakayama, 1984), critical flicker frequency (Hartmann et al., 1979), texture segmentation (Gurnsey et al., 1996; Barbot and Carrasco, 2017), and perceptual grouping (Tannazzo et al., 2014) do not show the same systematic decline with eccentricity as acuity.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Critical flicker frequency does not show the same systematic decline with eccentricity as acuity.
source: Other tasks such as motion sensitivity (McKee and Nakayama, 1984), critical flicker frequency (Hartmann et al., 1979), texture segmentation (Gurnsey et al., 1996; Barbot and Carrasco, 2017), and perceptual grouping (Tannazzo et al., 2014) do not show the same systematic decline with eccentricity as acuity.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

source: Other tasks such as motion sensitivity (McKee and Nakayama, 1984), critical flicker frequency (Hartmann et al., 1979), texture segmentation (Gurnsey et al., 1996; Barbot and Carrasco, 2017), and perceptual grouping (Tannazzo et al., 2014) do not show the same systematic decline with eccentricity as acuity.

claim: For tasks that do not show systematic decline with eccentricity, performance might be less tightly linked to V1 surface area.
source: For these tasks, performance might be less tightly linked to V1 surface area.
evidence: Speculation based on differences in task properties.

claim: The overall size of V1 and the cortical magnification function correlate with vernier acuity.
source: The overall size of V1 and the cortical magnification function (averaged across polar angles) correlate with various measures of perception, including vernier acuity (Duncan and Boynton, 2003; Song et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The overall size of V1 and the cortical magnification function correlate with perceived angular size.
source: perceived angular size (Murray et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: The overall size of V1 and the cortical magnification function correlate with the strength of some illusions.
source: and the strength of some illusions (Schwarzkopf et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: The cortical HVA and VMA in individuals may predict radial asymmetries in their visual performance.
source: The cortical HVA and VMA in individuals may similarly predict radial asymmetries in their visual performance.
evidence: Speculation based on group-level correlations.

claim: The cone density is greatest in the fovea, falling off with increasing eccentricity.
source: This finding that polar angle asymmetries are larger across successive stages of visual processing parallels findings regarding eccentricity: the cone density is greatest in the fovea, falling off with increasing eccentricity (Curcio et al., 1990)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: The fall-off of cone density with eccentricity becomes steeper in the midget ganglion cell array.
source: this fall-off with eccentricity becomes steeper in the midget ganglion cell array (Curcio and Allen, 1990; Dacey, 1993; Watson, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The fall-off of cone density with eccentricity becomes steeper still in V1.
source: and steeper still in V1 (Adams and Horton, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study.

claim: The increases in the foveal bias and the radial asymmetries likely have important implications for visual performance.
source: Given that most human visual perception relies on signals passing through V1, the increases in the foveal bias and the radial asymmetries (HVA and VMA) likely have important implications for visual performance.
evidence: Inference based on the role of V1 in visual processing.

claim: The VMA falls off sharply with distance from the vertical meridian: the size of the VMA within 10° of the vertical meridian is ~80%, whereas within 40° it is only ~10%.
source: The VMA falls off sharply with distance from the vertical meridian: the size of the VMA within 10° of the vertical meridian is ~80%, whereas within 40° it is only ~10%.
evidence: Data from Figure 2E showing VMA as a function of angular distance.

claim: Assessing the relation between cortical area and behavior requires measurement at a fine angular resolution and in a large dataset.
source: Hence assessing the relation between cortical area and behavior requires measurement at a fine angular resolution and in a large dataset.
evidence: Inference based on methodological considerations and comparison with prior work.

claim: The boundaries drawn by four trained raters were incredibly reliable, with differences between raters accounting for <5% of all variance across subjects and raters.

To summarize: these boundaries are incredibly reliable, with differences between raters accounting for <5% of all variance across subjects and raters.
